cases.question: How long is an access token valid?
cases.criterion: the token is valid for sixty minutes
cases.kept: An access token is valid for sixty minutes from the moment it is issued, so long-running jobs should renew rather than hold one open.
cases.lost: Access tokens are short lived by design. Long-running jobs are expected to renew them periodically rather than holding a single token open for the whole run.

cases.question: What does AUTH-401 mean?
cases.criterion: AUTH-401 covers a missing, malformed or expired token
cases.kept: AUTH-401 is returned when the Authorization header is missing, malformed, or expired. The body names which of the three it was.
cases.lost: AUTH-401 indicates that the request was not authorised. The response body explains which part of the header the service objected to, so check that first.

cases.question: How many requests may a project make per minute?
cases.criterion: the limit is six hundred requests per minute
cases.kept: The default budget is six hundred requests per minute per project, counted across every environment together.
cases.lost: Each project has a request budget measured in a sliding window and counted across all environments together. Exceeding it returns RATE-429 with a Retry-After header.

cases.question: How long do refresh tokens last?
cases.kept: A refresh token lives for thirty days and is exchanged for a new access token at the renew endpoint.
cases.lost: Refresh tokens are long lived and single use: each renewal returns both a new access token and a new refresh token, and the old one is discarded immediately.

cases.question: What is the clock tolerance before TS-999?
cases.kept: TS-999 means the request timestamp differs from the service clock by more than five minutes.
cases.lost: TS-999 is a clock drift error. It is almost never a bug in your code - it is usually a container host or a suspended virtual machine whose clock has drifted.

cases.question: How long is a deleted record recoverable?
cases.criterion: a deleted record can be restored for thirty days
cases.kept: A deleted record is hidden immediately and destroyed thirty days later; it can be restored during that window.
cases.lost: Deletion is staged rather than immediate. There is a recovery window during which the record can be restored, after which restoration is genuinely impossible because it is removed from backups too.

cases.question: How many records fit in one batch write?
cases.criterion: a batch may contain up to five hundred records
cases.kept: Up to five hundred records can be submitted in a single call, and the whole submission either succeeds or fails.
cases.lost: Batch writes are all-or-nothing: there is no state in which only some of the records were written, and a submission over the limit is rejected rather than truncated.

cases.question: How often are encryption keys rotated?
cases.criterion: keys are rotated every ninety days
cases.kept: Keys are held in a separate service and rotated every ninety days, without downtime.
cases.lost: Keys live in a dedicated key service rather than on the machines serving requests, and rotation happens without downtime and without re-encrypting existing data.

cases.question: How long is the audit trail retained?
cases.criterion: the audit trail is kept for four hundred days
cases.kept: Audit entries are retained for four hundred days and can be exported.
cases.lost: Every write, permission change and issued token is recorded with the actor, the time and the calling address. The trail is append only and cannot be edited through the API.

cases.question: How many items does a listing return at a time?
cases.criterion: a listing returns one hundred items at a time
cases.kept: Collections return at most one hundred items at a time, with a cursor for the next page.
cases.lost: Listings are paginated with a cursor that encodes a position rather than an offset, so records inserted mid-listing will not cause you to skip or repeat an item.

cases.question: How long is an idempotency key remembered?
cases.criterion: idempotency keys are remembered for twenty four hours
cases.kept: Idempotency keys are remembered for twenty four hours; the same key returns the original result.
cases.lost: Supply an idempotency key on any call that creates something. If the same key arrives again the original result is returned rather than a second object being made.

cases.question: How much storage may one project hold?
cases.criterion: a project may hold fifty gigabytes
cases.kept: A project may hold up to ten million records and fifty gigabytes in total.
cases.lost: Projects have both a record count limit and a total size limit. Reaching either stops writes but never stops reads, so the application keeps serving users while somebody fixes it.
